What is session hijacking in one line?
column2: Stealing or riding an already-authenticated session so you skip the login — you become the user without the password.

#separator:: CEH's primary dividing line for hijacking?
column2: Network-level (TCP/IP session) vs. application-level (session token/cookie).

#separator:: Network-level hijacking attacks what?
column2: The TCP/IP session itself (SEQ/ACK, packets), not the app token.

#separator:: Application-level hijacking attacks what?
column2: The application session token/cookie (e.g. PHPSESSID).

#separator:: TCP sequence prediction — how does it work?
column2: Guess or observe the next SEQ/ACK numbers to inject packets as the client into an established session.

#separator:: Why is blind TCP hijacking hard on modern OSes?
column2: They randomize the initial sequence number (ISN), so an off-path attacker can't reliably predict SEQ.

#separator:: What is session desynchronization?
column2: Forcing client and server SEQ numbers out of sync so the attacker's injected packets are accepted and the real client's are dropped (ACK storm).

#separator:: What is RST hijacking, and its side effect?
column2: Forging a TCP RST with the right SEQ to tear down a peer's connection; it doubles as a DoS primitive.

#separator:: Blind vs. non-blind hijacking?
column2: Blind = attacker is off-path and must predict SEQ (harder); non-blind = MITM can see the traffic.

#separator:: Why is UDP hijacking easier than TCP?
column2: UDP is connectionless — no handshake or sequence numbers to defeat; just race a spoofed reply before the server.

#separator:: What is IP spoofing's role in hijacking?
column2: Forging the source IP to impersonate the client — a prerequisite for many network-level hijacks.

#separator:: The TCP three-way handshake being abused?
column2: SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK; hijacking injects into the established session by getting SEQ/ACK right.

#separator:: Sidejacking is what?
column2: Capturing a session cookie off an unencrypted or downgraded link (the classic Firesheep scenario).

#separator:: What kills sidejacking / token sniffing?
column2: TLS everywhere (plus HSTS) and the Secure cookie flag.

#separator:: How does XSS-based cookie theft work?
column2: Injected script reads document.cookie and exfiltrates it to the attacker.

#separator:: Which cookie flag blocks XSS cookie theft?
column2: HttpOnly — it prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie.

#separator:: What is session fixation?
column2: Attacker sets/knows the victim's session ID before login; victim authenticates it; attacker reuses the now-valid ID.

#separator:: What defeats session fixation?
column2: Regenerate (rotate) the session ID on authentication and on privilege change.

#separator:: Fixation vs. theft — the trap?
column2: Fixation = attacker supplies the ID up front; theft = attacker captures an ID the victim already has.

#separator:: What makes session IDs predictable, and the fix?
column2: Sequential/low-entropy IDs let an attacker guess a valid one; fix = long, high-entropy random tokens in a server-side store.

#separator:: How does CSRF relate to hijacking?
column2: CSRF makes the victim's browser send an authenticated request — it rides the session but never sees/steals the token.

#separator:: Which cookie flag curbs CSRF?
column2: SameSite (plus anti-CSRF tokens).

#separator:: Which cookie flag stops a cookie crossing non-TLS?
column2: Secure.

#separator:: Hijacking vs. spoofing vs. replay?
column2: Hijacking takes over a live authenticated session (no password); spoofing forges identity to initiate; replay resends captured data.

#separator:: Active vs. passive hijacking?
column2: Active = take over the live session and push the user out (desync/RST); passive = observe/record and replay the token later.

#separator:: MITM position — how to get it on a LAN?
column2: ARP spoofing/poisoning, DNS spoofing, or a rogue access point.

#separator:: What is SSL stripping and its counter?
column2: Downgrading HTTPS to HTTP at a MITM to read cookies; countered by HSTS.

#separator:: Tool: intercept/replay HTTP session tokens & test fixation?
column2: Burp Suite.

#separator:: Tool: Follow TCP Stream to read cookies/SEQ numbers?
column2: Wireshark.

#separator:: Tools for ARP-poison MITM on a LAN?
column2: ettercap and bettercap.

#separator:: Why does PSM (PAM broker) blunt session hijacking?
column2: The privileged session runs on the broker, not the endpoint — there's no local token/cookie to steal, and it can be killed live.

#separator:: PAM controls that shrink a hijack window?
column2: Session brokering + recording, step-up re-auth (MFA) for sensitive actions, short idle timeouts, token rotation on privilege change, session binding.
